beats.say: Hi! Every photo and every sentence you post on social media is information for someone. Let us look at it together.
An office photo can show your badge, an open screen or whiteboard notes. That is ready material for an attack.
Do not announce trips in advance: it tells everyone your home is empty and you are hard to reach. Post photos afterwards.
Fake profiles exist too. A recruiter with a dream job may be gathering facts about your organisation. Check the profile's age.

body.text: Hello! I saw your profile. A high-paying job abroad would suit you perfectly.

options.label: A selfie at the office with my new badge
options.feedback: The badge design, your name and your role are visible. That is a ready template for a fake badge.

options.label: Off on a week of holiday from tomorrow
options.feedback: It tells people when your home is empty and when you cannot be reached.

options.label: A nature photo after I got back
options.feedback: Correct. The place and time are in the past, and nothing about work is visible.

options.label: My desk, with the monitor open behind
options.feedback: A document, email or system name on the screen can be read by zooming in.

scenes.explain: Before you post, check the background: badge, screen, whiteboard, papers.

scenes.prompt: Find the signs of a fake recruiter.

body.text: A job abroad paying 6000 dollars a month is waiting for you.
One quick question before the interview:
which email system and which software does your organisation use?
Fill in the form with your work email:
Places are limited, it closes today.

spots.label: New profile, few connections
spots.explain: Real recruiters usually have a long history and mutual contacts. A profile with three connections was just created.

spots.label: Too good to be true
spots.explain: A big salary before any interview is bait. Excitement lowers your guard.

spots.label: Questions about your organisation
spots.explain: A recruiter does not need your organisation's systems. This is reconnaissance for an attack.

spots.label: Outside link asking for work email
spots.explain: Entering your work email on an outside form puts it on a phishing list. The form may also ask for a password.

spots.label: Pressure to hurry
spots.explain: Closes today is there so you do not stop to think.

scenes.prompt: Is this message safe or a threat?

body.text: Hi! My daughter is in a contest, please vote for her. You will get a code by SMS, send it to me.

cards.explain: That code is the key to your account. Never share it, even if the message comes from a friend's account.

messages.text: New sign-in to your account: Baku, phone. If this was not you, open Security in the app.

cards.explain: No link and no code request, it sends you to the app itself. Do the check inside the app.

body.text: Hi, we work in the same field. Could you send me your head of department's mobile number?

cards.explain: A stranger is looking for a way to reach your manager. Give contact details only through official channels.

body.text: Tomorrow's meeting moved to 11, same room.

cards.explain: A known colleague, no request, nothing sensitive. This message is safe.

body.text: To verify your account, send your job title, work email and date of birth.

cards.explain: Official bodies do not ask for this on social media. Do not reply, and report the profile.

scenes.prompt: Match each setting to what it gives you.

pairs.right: No one sees where you are
No one can tag you without approval
The account stays safe even if the password leaks

scenes.explain: Check these settings from time to time. New app features can change them.

points: Check the background: badge, screen, papers.
Post trip photos after you return.
Never give work details or codes to strangers.
